mappings.note: The gaseous state of water is water vapour. Naming a state, LO-79.
Water to vapour is evaporation. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Water vapour is invisible. An observable -- or rather unobservable -- feature of a state, LO-79.
Give a daily-life example of evaporation. Recognising the process in everyday life, LO-88.
Hand sanitizer evaporates off the hands. The process met in a daily habit, LO-88.
The tiny drops on a cold tumbler are water droplets. Naming what is observed, LO-79.
Vapour to liquid is condensation. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
The water vapour in air is humidity. Naming a property of the air, LO-79.
The solid state of water is ice. Naming a state, LO-79.
Whether ice flows like water. A property contrast between two states, LO-80.
Liquid water has no fixed shape and takes the container's. A defining property set against the solid state, LO-80.
Gases have no fixed shape and fill the space available. A property of the gaseous state against the others, LO-80.
Name another substance existing in all three states. Extends the three-state classification beyond water, LO-81.
Heat must be supplied to turn ice into water. The cause of the change, LO-83.
Solid to liquid is melting. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Liquid to solid is freezing. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Name a condition that affects evaporation rate. A factor governing the process, LO-83.
Evaporation cools its surroundings. The effect the process causes, LO-83.
Circulation of water between surface and atmosphere is the water cycle. Naming the process, LO-84.
Whether ice and water are different substances or different states. Placing both in the same substance's state classification, LO-81.
Why water on a hot pan vanishes quickly. Heat as the cause of rapid evaporation, LO-83.
Why steam is visible when vapour is not -- some of it has condensed. Explaining a commonly misread phenomenon, LO-84.
How morning dew forms on leaves. Vapour meeting a cool surface as the cause, LO-83.
Ice keeps its own shape whatever the container. Describing an observable property of one state, LO-79; no comparison is demanded, so not LO-80.
Liquid water takes the container's shape but keeps its volume. One state's properties described, LO-79.
Vapour has no fixed shape and spreads to fill the space. One state's properties described, LO-79.
Ice to water to vapour by supplying heat. A chain of state changes explained, LO-84.
Water to ice by cooling, called freezing. Naming and explaining a change of state, LO-84.
How greater exposed area speeds evaporation. A factor governing the rate, with its mechanism, LO-83.
Sunlight against shade for evaporation rate. A factor governing the rate, LO-83.
How wind speeds drying -- it carries the vapour away. A factor with its mechanism, LO-83.
Why clothes dry slowly in the rain -- the air is already humid. A factor governing the rate, LO-83.
The matka's cooling explained through seepage and evaporation drawing heat. The causal chain, LO-83.
Another everyday use of evaporative cooling -- sprinkling water on a roof or floor. Applying the learning in daily life, LO-88.
How clouds form -- vapour rises, cools, condenses on dust. Explaining a stage of the water cycle, LO-84.
Droplets coalesce until too heavy and fall as rain. Explaining the next stage of the water cycle, LO-84.
Besides rain, condensed water falls as hail or snow. Sorting the forms precipitation takes, LO-81.
Why only a small share of Earth's water is usable -- most is saline. The scarcity argument that grounds conservation, LO-89.
What an Atmospheric Water Generator is and how it condenses drinkable water from humid air. A device whose working must be explained, LO-87; NEP content the frame does not name.
Describe evaporation and condensation with a daily example of each. Two processes explained, LO-84.
Compare the three states on shape, flow and spread. A three-way differentiation on properties, LO-80.
Three conditions that speed evaporation, each with how it works. Factors and their mechanisms, LO-83.
How the matka cools and the principle behind it. LO-83 for the causal chain; LO-87 because the pot is the chapter's worked device and the item asks how its construction produces the effect.
Cloud formation through to rain, as part of the water cycle. Explaining the process, LO-84.
The three states and every transition between them, named. The full set of state-change processes explained, LO-84.
Describe an activity that EVIDENCES invisible water vapour in the air. The item asks for an investigation that supplies evidence, LO-82.
Why to use water wisely, two ways it gets polluted, and why that matters. Protecting the environment and spreading awareness of judicious use, LO-89.
The common cause of vanishing puddles and drying utensils, plus the extra factor for puddles -- seepage. Distinguishing two causes of one observation, LO-83.
How humidity affects evaporation and why clothes dry slowly when it is high. A factor with its mechanism, LO-83.
Clothes drying faster in sun and wind, and spread out. LO-83 for the three factors and their mechanisms, LO-88 because the item is a household practice reasoned about.
Droplets on a cold bottle while the level inside is unchanged. Part (iii) forces the correct causal attribution -- external air, not seepage -- LO-83.

Coconut oil solidifying in winter and melting when warmed, and whether it behaves like water. Placing a second substance in the same reversible change-of-state classification, LO-81's own example of changes that can be reversed.
The gardener sprinkling water to cool the path. LO-88 for the everyday practice, LO-83 for parts (i)-(ii), which explain the cooling and why a dry day helps more.
Steam rising and droplets forming on a cool lid, then identifying the two states. Naming and explaining both changes of state, LO-84.
